CHAPTER V

Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was an artful man. He opened on the novice with
something quite wide of the mark he was really aiming at. “The town
records,” said he, “are crabbedly written, and the ink rusty with age.”
 He offered Gerard the honour of transcribing them fair.

Gerard inquired what he was to be paid.

Ghysbrecht offered a sum that would have just purchased the pens, ink,
and parchment.

“But, burgomaster, my labour? Here is a year's work.”

“Your labour? Call you marking parchment labour? Little sweat goes to
that, I trow.”

“'Tis labour, and skilled labour to boot; and that is better paid in all
crafts than rude labour, sweat or no sweat. Besides, there's my time.”

“Your time? Why, what is time to you, at two-and-twenty?” Then fixing
his eyes keenly on Gerard, to mark the effect of his words, he said:
“Say, rather, you are idle grown. You are in love. Your body is with
these chanting monks, but your heart is with Peter Brandt and his
red-haired girl.”

“I know no Peter Brandt.”

This denial confirmed Ghysbrecht's suspicion that the caster-out of
demons was playing a deep game.

“Ye lie!” he shouted. “Did I not find you at her elbow on the road to
Rotterdam?”

“Ah!”

“Ah! And you were seen at Sevenbergen but t'other day.”

“Was I?'

“Ah and at Peter's house.”

“At Sevenbergen?”

“Ay, at Sevenbergen.”

Now, this was what in modern days is called a draw. It was a guess, put
boldly forth as fact, to elicit by the young man's answer whether he had
been there lately or not.

The result of the artifice surprised the crafty one. Gerard started up
in a strange state of nervous excitement.

“Burgomaster,” said he, with trembling voice, “I have not been at
Sevenbergen these three years, and I know not the name of those you saw
me with, nor where they dwelt; but, as my time is precious, though
you value it not, give you good day.” And he darted out, with his eyes
sparkling.

Ghysbrecht started up in huge ire; but he sank into his chair again.

“He fears me not. He knows something, if not all.”

Then he called hastily to his trusty servant, and almost dragged him to
a window.

“See you yon man?” he cried. “Haste! follow him! But let him not see
you. He is young, but old in craft. Keep him in sight all day. Let me
know whither he goes, and what he does.”

It was night when the servant returned.

“Well? well?” cried Van Swieten eagerly.

“Master, the young man went from you to Sevenbergen.”

Ghysbrecht groaned.

“To the house of Peter the Magician.”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

generated_text:
Ghysbrecht Van Swieten was a man of calculated artistry, a strategist who understood that the most effective trap is often disguised as an offer. He approached the novice with a bait that deliberately missed its mark, casting a line far wider than the hook he truly sought to set.

"The town records," he began, his voice smooth as polished oak, "are crabbedly written, the ink rusted by the slow corrosion of centuries." With a gesture that feigned benevolence, he extended the honor of transcription to Gerard. "You shall make them fair."

Gerard, ever pragmatic, inquired immediately of the wage. Ghysbrecht named a sum so meager it covered merely the cost of pens, ink, and parchment.

"But, Burgomaster," Gerard pressed, his tone sharpening, "what of my labor? Consider this a year's work."

"Your labor?" Ghysbrecht scoffed, a dismissive curl touching his lip. "Do you call the mere marking of parchment 'labor'? A little sweat goes to that, I trow."

"'Tis labor," Gerard countered, his stance firm despite the weight of the older man's presence, "and skilled labor to boot. In every craft, skill is valued higher than brute toil, regardless of the sweat shed. Furthermore, there is the matter of my time."

"Your time?" Ghysbrecht laughed softly, the sound devoid of warmth. "Why, what is time to you, at twenty-two?"

Fixing his eyes upon Gerard with a keen, predatory intensity designed to gauge the tremor in the boy's resolve, he delivered the blow. "Say, rather, you have grown idle. You are in love. Your body remains among these chanting monks, but your heart belongs to Peter Brandt and his red-haired girl."

"I know no Peter Brandt."

The denial only hardened Ghysbrecht's suspicion that the exorcist was playing a deeper, more dangerous game than he admitted.

"Ye lie!" Ghysbrecht roared, the mask of civility shattering. "Did I not find you at her elbow on the road to Rotterdam?"

"Aha!"

"And you were seen at Sevenbergen but the other day."

"Was I?"

"Aha! And at Peter's house."

"At Sevenbergen?"

"Aye, at Sevenbergen."

In the lexicon of modern intrigue, this maneuver constitutes a bold draw—a guess presented as undeniable fact, intended to force the subject's hand and reveal the truth through their reaction. The result of this psychological stratagem surpassed even the crafty Burgomaster's expectations.

Gerard sprang to his feet, seized by a strange, electric state of nervous excitation.

"Burgomaster," he said, his voice trembling not with fear, but with a fierce, defiant clarity, "I have not been to Sevenbergen these three years. I know not the names of those you claim to have seen me with, nor where they dwell. But since my time is precious—even if you choose to squander it—I bid you good day."

With a sudden, darting motion, he turned and fled, his eyes sparkling with a light that suggested not defeat, but revelation.

Ghysbrecht surged upward in a fit of huge, blinding ire, only to sink slowly back into his chair, the rage cooling into a colder, more calculating dread.

"He fears me not," he muttered, tracing the rim of his cup. "He knows something. If not everything, certainly enough to unsettle me."

Then, summoning his trusty servant with a hurried command, he almost dragged the man to the window.

"Do you see yon man?" Ghysbrecht cried, pointing a shaking finger toward the street below. "Haste! Follow him! But ensure he sees nothing of you. He is young, yes, but old in craft. Keep him in sight all day. Tell me whither he goes, and what he does."

Night had fallen when the servant returned, breathless and urgent.

"Well? Well?" Ghysbrecht demanded, leaning forward eagerly.

"Master," the servant replied, his voice low, "the young man went from here... straight to Sevenbergen."

Ghysbrecht let out a long, mournful groan that echoed in the silent room.

"To the house of Peter the Magician."
